summary: Defines the Internationalized Resource Identifier (IRI), a complement to the URI built from characters in the Unicode universal character set. It defines a mapping from IRIs to URIs, so IRIs can be used where URIs are required.

plainLanguage.summary: A web address that can use letters from any language, with a rule to turn it into a plain form old computers understand.

questions: how to convert an iri to a uri
subtitle: Web-style identifiers that can use characters from any script, with a fixed rule for turning them into plain URIs.

tldr.problem: URIs are limited to a small subset of US-ASCII, even though people often want to write identifiers in the characters of their own language.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3987 defines the IRI, a URI-like identifier made of Unicode (ISO 10646) characters, and a deterministic mapping that turns any IRI into a URI by encoding non-ASCII characters as UTF-8 and percent-encoding the octets.
tldr.outcome: IRIs can be used instead of URIs where a protocol or format is designed to carry them. Where only URIs are allowed, such as the HTTP request URI, the IRI must be mapped first.

today: RFC 3987 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2005, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why IRIs Exist
sections.content:
A URI, as defined in RFC 3986, is a sequence of characters from a limited subset of US-ASCII. Yet URI characters often spell words of natural languages, which makes them easier to remember, type and guess. For most languages other than English the natural script is not A to Z, and transcribing into Latin letters introduces ambiguities.

RFC 3987 defines a new protocol element, the Internationalized Resource Identifier (IRI), by extending URI syntax to a much wider character repertoire. The authors chose a new element instead of changing the URI definition, so that the two stay clearly distinct and existing software is not broken.

IRIs are for contexts that are designed to accept them. The RFC gives the example that XML Schema's anyURI type includes IRIs, whereas the HTTP request URI is defined as a URI, so IRIs cannot be used directly in HTTP requests. A protocol that carries IRIs also needs a way to represent the wide range of characters, and the corresponding URI has to encode original characters as UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: Web addresses used to be limited to plain English letters. IRIs let you write an address in your own alphabet, like writing a letter in your own language.

sections.title: IRI Syntax
sections.content:
An IRI is a sequence of characters, not of octets, so it can be written on paper or read over the radio as well as stored digitally. Its grammar closely follows the URI grammar. The set of unreserved characters is extended with the characters of the Universal Character Set (UCS) beyond U+007F, which the ABNF calls ucschar.

Most rules get an i prefix: iauthority, ipath, iquery, ifragment, ireg-name and so on. Private-use UCS characters (iprivate) may appear only in the query part.

Everything else works as for URIs: components, reserved characters and relative-reference resolution behave the same way. Because characters outside US-ASCII are not reserved, they MUST NOT be used as delimiters in newly defined schemes. The syntax does not support IPv6 scoped addressing zone identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: An IRI is built like a normal web address, but the building blocks are allowed to be letters from any writing system.

sections.title: Mapping an IRI to a URI
sections.content:
Applications MUST map IRIs to URIs in two steps. Step 1 produces a UCS character sequence from whatever form the IRI was in. Text on paper or read aloud is represented in Normalization Form C (NFC), as is text converted from a non-Unicode encoding. An IRI already in a Unicode encoding such as UTF-8 or UTF-16 is not normalized.

Step 2 takes each character in ucschar or iprivate, converts it to octets using UTF-8 (RFC 3629), writes each octet as %HH and substitutes the result. The hexadecimal digits SHOULD be uppercase. The result is a valid URI. The mapping leaves URIs unchanged and is idempotent, so every URI is by definition an IRI.

Existing percent-encoded sequences and characters already allowed in URIs are not encoded again. For hosts, a system MAY instead apply the ToASCII operation of RFC 3490 to each label of the registered name, for schemes that use domain names there. The RFC's example turns a host with e-acute characters in "resume" into an xn--rsum-bpad label rather than %C3%A9 escapes. This is recommended when maximizing interoperability with legacy URI resolvers.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like spelling a word with fancy letters out loud using a code every telephone operator knows, so the message gets through even on an old line.

sections.title: Going Back and Using UTF-8
sections.content:
Converting a URI to an IRI is optional and follows five steps: treat the URI as US-ASCII octets, decode percent-encodings except those for %, reserved characters and US-ASCII characters not allowed in URIs, re-encode any octets that are not strictly legal UTF-8, re-encode characters that are not appropriate in an IRI, and read the result as UTF-8. Conversions MUST NOT guess any encoding other than UTF-8, even when context suggests one.

The RFC illustrates the reason with a URI containing %E9. It might be e-acute in iso-8859-1, but if it were turned into an IRI that character, it would later map back to %C3%A9, which is a different URI.

Because of this, an IRI only corresponds to a URI whose percent-encoding was UTF-8 based. This explains why most existing URI schemes need no upgrade, though schemes limited to US-ASCII with no percent-encoding of non-ASCII, like mailto:, might. The RFC also notes that there is no such thing as an "IRI scheme": all IRIs use URI schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: You can sometimes turn the coded address back into pretty letters, but only if you are sure which code book was used. If you guess wrong, you end up at a different address.

sections.title: Right-to-Left Scripts
sections.content:
Characters in Arabic and Hebrew run right to left, so IRIs containing them (bidirectional IRIs) must handle the gap between logical order, used for storage and spelling, and visual order, used for display. When stored or sent, a bidirectional IRI MUST be in full logical order and conform to the IRI syntax. It MUST be rendered with the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm, as if inside a left-to-right embedding.

IRIs MUST NOT contain bidirectional formatting characters such as LRM, RLM, LRE, RLE, LRO, RLO and PDF, since they change how the IRI is displayed without being part of it.

To keep display predictable, each component (such as a host label or path segment) SHOULD NOT mix right-to-left and left-to-right characters, and a component using right-to-left characters SHOULD start and end with them. Numbers at the start or end of such a component can be misread, for instance a sequence such as 1/2 being treated as a fraction. If the restrictions cannot be met, the whole component can be mapped to URI notation.
sections.plainLanguage: Some languages are written from right to left. The rules make sure an address looks the same to everyone and does not get scrambled on screen.

sections.title: Comparing and Normalizing IRIs
sections.content:
Comparison is done by string comparison, possibly with extra rules from scheme definitions, and it is designed to minimize false negatives while strictly avoiding false positives. Applications that use IRIs as plain identity tokens with no relation to a protocol MUST use simple string comparison. All others pick a step from the comparison ladder, which trades more processing for fewer false negatives.

  • Simple string comparison: identical character strings are equivalent. Comparison must be done character by character after converting to a common encoding, and MUST NOT map IRIs to URIs.
  • Syntax-based normalization: case normalization (uppercase hex digits in percent-encodings, lowercase scheme and ASCII host), percent-encoding normalization, and removing dot-segments.
  • Scheme-based normalization: for example, http://example.com and http://example.com:80/ are equivalent, and internationalized domain names can be compared with their punycode forms.
  • Protocol-based normalization: for example, a web spider that sees a redirect that only adds a trailing slash may treat the two as equivalent later.

Equivalence of IRIs MUST rely on IRIs being pre-character-normalized, and IRIs SHOULD be created using NFC. Normalization used for comparison should only be performed locally. If the IRI is passed on, its original form MUST be preserved.
sections.plainLanguage: To decide whether two addresses mean the same place, you can just check if they are spelled exactly the same, or do extra tidying first. More tidying catches more matches but takes more work.

sections.title: Using IRIs in Software
sections.content:
Software interfaces and protocols MUST define which character encoding they use. Components that carry IRIs to URI-only components MUST map them as in section 3, and SHOULD apply the mapping as late as possible and not between components that can handle IRIs. In a document with its own native character encoding, IRIs MUST use that encoding, and characters it cannot express SHOULD be escaped using the format's conventions, such as numeric character references in HTML or XML.

An informative section gives guidelines for entering, transferring, generating, selecting and displaying IRIs. Examples are that programs spotting links in plain text should not treat a non-ASCII character as the end of an IRI, servers should expose file names as UTF-8 percent-encoded URIs, publishers should avoid confusable characters and prefer NFKC, and parts the display cannot render correctly should be percent-encoded. It also suggests upgrading interpreting software first, then entry and transport software, and generating IRIs only once services accept them.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs should agree on which alphabet code they use, and only change an address into its plain coded form at the last moment, when they have to.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3986 also apply. Two additional problems stand out. First, incorrect encoding or decoding can cause trouble. Some UTF-8 decoders do not reject overlong sequences, so 0xC0 0xAF might be wrongly read as /, and a string such as %C0%AF.. could pass a security check and then be interpreted as /...

Second, spoofing: someone adds a resource name that looks the same or similar to the user but points elsewhere. In the UCS many characters look very similar, such as the Latin "A", the Greek "Alpha" and the Cyrillic "A". Spoofing can also come from mismatched normalization between the user's input and the server, from accepting percent-encodings in several character encodings for older user agents, and from bidirectional IRIs that break the restrictions in section 4.2. A correct Unicode bidirectional implementation is very important.
sections.plainLanguage: Many letters from different alphabets look alike, so a trickster could make a fake address that looks just like the real one. Programs have to be careful about this.
